title: Real-Time Streaming Protocol Version 2.0
summary: RTSP 2.0 is an application-layer protocol for setting up and controlling delivery of real-time data such as audio and video, from live feeds or stored clips. It is an extensible framework for controlled, on-demand delivery. This standards-track RFC obsoletes RTSP 1.0 from RFC 2326.

plainLanguage.summary: RTSP is a way to control a media server over a network. A player asks what is on offer, sets up the delivery channels, then plays, pauses or stops. The control messages are plain text over TCP or TLS, and the audio and video travel separately, usually as RTP.

questions: how does rtsp control streaming media
what is the default rtsp port
subtitle: A network remote control for streaming servers: set up a session, then play, pause, seek and tear down media that travels by other means.

tldr.problem: A client that wants to watch or listen to media on a server needs a standard way to find out what is on offer, to agree how the media will be delivered, and then to start, stop and reposition it.
tldr.mechanism: RTSP 2.0 is a text-based request and response protocol carried over TCP or TLS. The client describes, sets up and plays a session with methods such as DESCRIBE, SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE and TEARDOWN, while the media itself is delivered separately, usually as RTP.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track replacement for RTSP 1.0 from RFC 2326 and is deliberately not backwards compatible apart from the version negotiation. It drops the RECORD and ANNOUNCE methods and RTSP over UDP, and adds request pipelining, IPv6 support and server-to-client notifications.

today: RFC 7826 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2326 (RTSP 1.0), and no other RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Network address translation for RTSP 2.0 is specified separately in RFC 7825.

sections.title: What RTSP 2.0 Is For
sections.content:
RFC 7826 defines version 2.0 of the Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP). RTSP is an application-layer protocol for setting up and controlling the delivery of data with real-time properties, such as video on demand or live audio streaming. The RFC calls it a network remote control for multimedia servers.

The protocol runs between RTSP clients and servers, and it also supports proxies placed in between. A client can request information about streaming media from a server by asking for a description of the media, or it can use a media description provided from outside. The media delivery protocol is then used to establish the media streams that the description names. Clients can ask the server to play the media out, to pause it, or to stop it completely. The requested media can consist of several audio and video streams, delivered as time-synchronized streams from the server to the client.

RTSP 2.0 replaces RTSP 1.0 from RFC 2326 and obsoletes it. It is based on RTSP 1.0 but is not backwards compatible other than in the basic version negotiation. The RFC gives four main reasons: headers that needed to be extensible did not define the allowed syntax, the changed behaviour of the PLAY method when it is received in the Play state, the changed behaviour of the extensibility model, and a change in the syntax of some headers. It says there were so many small updates that changing versions became necessary to allow clarification and consistent behaviour, and that anyone implementing RTSP for a new use case, with no RTSP 1.0 already installed, should implement only RTSP 2.0.

Appendix I lists the differences. RTSP 2.0 removed the RECORD and ANNOUNCE methods and everything attached to them, removed the use of UDP for RTSP message transport, and removed the use of the PLAY method as a keep-alive in the Play state. It added a TEARDOWN from server to client, the asynchronous PLAY_NOTIFY method, IPv6 support, extended IANA registries, request pipelining for a quicker session start, a fully reworked state machine, the use of URIs rather than URLs, and an expanded REDIRECT method.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP lets a player on one machine control a media server on another: ask what is on offer, set up the channels, then play, pause or stop. The audio and video are sent separately from the control messages.

sections.title: How an RTSP Session Works
sections.content:
RTSP has three fundamental parts: session establishment, media delivery control, and an extensibility model. It is a bidirectional request and response protocol. Clients send requests, and servers can send requests to clients as well. Messages are text, with a possible binary message body, and they travel over a reliable transport. RTSP 2.0 requires clients and servers to implement TCP, and TLS over TCP, as the mandatory transports for RTSP messages.

RTSP does not describe the media itself. A presentation description says how many media streams there are, the resource identifier for each stream that RTSP is to control, the protocol that will deliver each stream, the transport parameters that are not negotiated or that vary from client to client, the encoding information a client needs to decode the media, and an aggregate control resource identifier. The description arrives either out of band or as the body of the response to a DESCRIBE request. Appendix D describes how to use the Session Description Protocol (SDP) for this purpose.

The client then sends a SETUP request. In the Transport header it lists the delivery alternatives it can accept, in decreasing order of preference, and the server picks one, creates an RTSP session and returns a session identifier in the Session header. A further SETUP that names the same session adds another media resource to it. A session with several streams is an aggregated session, controlled through one aggregate control URI, so that a single PLAY or PAUSE acts on the audio and the video together.

To save a round trip, the client can pipeline the requests that set up and start a session, sending them back to back without waiting for the first answer. The Pipelined-Requests header binds them together as if they had carried the session identifier. This speeds up the start of a session by at least one round trip.

A session stays alive while the client shows liveness, either with any RTSP request that carries the session or with RTCP reports when RTP carries the media. The default session timeout is 60 seconds, and the server can set another value in the timeout parameter of the Session header. The client normally ends the session by sending a TEARDOWN request to the aggregate control URI. If all media resources are removed from a session, the session is terminated.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first asks what the server has, then asks for the delivery channels to be set up, and then starts playback. The server answers each request with a session number that the client quotes in every later request.

sections.title: URI Schemes, Session Identifiers and Feature Tags
sections.content:
RTSP 2.0 defines and registers three URI schemes. With rtsp, commands travel over a reliable transport, which within the Internet is TCP, and the default port is 554. With rtsps, the transport is TLS and the default port is 322. The rtspu scheme exists only to register the scheme that RTSP 1.0 defined; its use is unspecified in RTSP 2.0, and a server must answer a request carrying an rtspu URI with 501 (Not Implemented). The RFC also records an alternative registered port, 8554, for servers that cannot use the default ports.

A request identifies its resource with an absolute RTSP URI, including scheme, host and port, rather than with just a path as in HTTP. A URI may name one stream, such as rtsp://media.example.com:554/twister/audiotrack, or the whole presentation, such as rtsp://media.example.com:554/twister. The path components are opaque to the client and imply nothing about the file system on the server. RTSP 2.0 also allows an IPv6 literal in the host part, which RTSP 1.0 did not support.

Every request carries a CSeq number. It maps responses to requests, and a proxy that serves several clients over one connection rewrites it so that it can tell the responses apart.

A session identifier is a string of 8 to 128 characters. It must be generated in a cryptographically random way, and the RFC recommends 128 bits of entropy, which is about 22 characters from a high-quality generator. The identifier does not by itself protect the session against hijacking, because that requires the client, the server and any trusted proxy to keep it confidential.

Extensions are handled through feature tags, which are unique identifiers naming a block of functionality. The Supported header lists what a party can do. The Require header names a feature the receiver must understand, and the request then fails with 551 (Option Not Supported) if the feature is missing. Proxy-Require applies the same rule to proxies only, and Unsupported lists the features that were missing. The tag play.basic stands for the whole minimal playback functionality of this specification, and it does not mandate any media delivery protocol such as RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RTSP address starts with a scheme that says how the control messages travel: rtsp for plain TCP, rtsps for TLS. The server also hands out a long random session number that the client quotes in every later request.

sections.title: Media Properties and Media Time Formats
sections.content:
Positions in the media are given in the Range header, in one of three time formats. Normal Play Time (NPT) is the position relative to the start of the presentation, such as npt=123.45-125, and the special value now means the current instant of a live event. SMPTE time codes give frame-level offsets from the start of the clip, and the default format is SMPTE 30 drop at 29.97 frames per second. Absolute time uses a UTC timestamp such as clock=19961108T143720.25Z-19961108T144725.25Z. A range covers its start point and excludes its end point.

What a client may do depends on the media. The server describes the content in the Media-Properties header of the SETUP response, using independent attributes:

  • Random access: Random-Access, Beginning-Only or No-Seeking. With Random-Access the server may also give the worst-case distance in seconds to the nearest reachable point.
  • Retention: Unlimited, Time-Limited or Time-Duration.
  • Content modification: Immutable, Dynamic or Time-Progressing.
  • Scales: the list of playback scales the content supports.

The RFC maps the common cases onto these attributes. On-demand media is Random-Access with Immutable content and Unlimited or Time-Limited retention. Dynamic on-demand media, such as a playlist, is Random-Access with Dynamic content. Live media is No-Seeking with Time-Progressing content and Time-Duration=0.0. Live media with recording adds Random-Access and a longer Time-Duration.

Live media cannot be seeked, so a client plays npt=now-. For live content that is being recorded, the Media-Range header tells the client how much is currently available, and a server that keeps only a recent window moves the start of that window forward as time passes. A pause point that falls outside the retained window is moved to the oldest retained position.

Two headers change the pace. Scale is the ratio of media time delivered per unit of playback time: 2.0 is fast forward, values between 0 and 1.0 are slow motion, negative values play backwards, and 0 is not allowed. Speed is the ratio of playback time delivered per unit of wallclock time, which lets a client fill its buffer faster than it plays; a value of 0 is not allowed. The two act on different timescales, and their effects combine.
sections.plainLanguage: Time in the media can be counted from the start of the programme, by frame number, or by the wall clock. The server also says whether the media can be seeked to any point, as a stored film can, or only watched as it arrives, as a live broadcast does.

sections.title: The RTSP Message
sections.content:
RTSP is a text-based protocol that uses the ISO 10646 character set in UTF-8, and every line is terminated by a CRLF. A request carries a method, the resource the method acts on and the protocol version; a response carries the version, a status code and a reason phrase. Both are followed by zero or more header fields, an empty line, and possibly a message body. Unknown headers must be ignored by clients and servers, and a proxy must forward them. A message body requires a Content-Length header, and RTSP does not support the HTTP chunked transfer coding.

A request line has the form <Method> SP <Request-URI> SP <RTSP-Version> CRLF. An asterisk may replace the URI to address the server or proxy itself, as in OPTIONS * RTSP/2.0, which reports the capabilities of the next hop. The version uses a major and a minor number. The minor number is incremented when the protocol gains features that do not change the message parsing algorithm, and the major number is incremented when the format of a message changes. RTSP/2.4 is a lower version than RTSP/2.13, which is lower than RTSP/12.3.

The general headers may be used in both requests and responses. They are Accept-Ranges, Cache-Control, Connection, CSeq, Date, Media-Properties, Media-Range, Pipelined-Requests, Proxy-Supported, Range, RTP-Info, Scale, Seek-Style, Server, Session, Speed, Supported, Timestamp, Transport, User-Agent and Via. Request-only headers include Accept, Accept-Credentials, Authorization, Bandwidth, Blocksize, From, If-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-None-Match, Notify-Reason, Proxy-Authorization, Proxy-Require, Referrer, Request-Status, Require and Terminate-Reason. Message body headers include Allow, Content-Base, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Location, Content-Type, Expires and Last-Modified.

A message body may be attached to any request or response, and the receiver may ignore its content. The format of the body is named in the Content-Type header, and the requester can use the Accept header to list the formats it understands. If none of them matches, the responder answers 406 (Not Acceptable). Formats are negotiated per method and per direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RTSP message is a short note: a first line that says what is wanted, some labelled lines of detail, and sometimes an attachment. Every note carries a number so that the reply can be matched to the question.

sections.title: Connections, Timeouts and Overload
sections.content:
RTSP 2.0 runs only over TCP, or over TCP with TLS. RFC 2326 attempted to specify an optional mechanism for carrying RTSP messages over a connectionless transport such as UDP, but it was not specified in enough detail to allow interoperable implementations, so RTSP 2.0 does not define one. One consequence is that RTSP requests must not be sent to multicast groups, because no connection can be established with a specific receiver in a multicast environment. Because the transport is reliable, RTSP messages must not be retransmitted at the RTSP level.

A server must handle both persistent connections, used for several exchanges, and transient connections, used for one. Persistent connections are recommended, partly because a server can only send requests to a client over a connection the client has opened. An agent may use one connection for several sessions on the same server, but must not use more than one connection per session at any one time. A server that tries to send a request to a client with no open connection must discard the request.

The RFC gives concrete timers. A responder should answer within 5 seconds; if it knows the work will take longer, it should send a 100 (Continue) response and repeat it every 5 seconds until the final answer. A requester should wait at least 10 seconds before concluding that no response is coming, and may then close the connection. A server should wait at least 10 seconds after answering the last session-level TEARDOWN before closing the connection, in case the client wants to set up a new session on it. For keep-alives, a SET_PARAMETER request without a body is the recommended method, and servers must support it. RTCP reports serve the same purpose when RTP carries the media.

When overloaded, servers answer 503 (Service Unavailable) and proxies answer 553 (Proxy Unavailable), both with a Retry-After header. The RFC requires the delay to grow in proportion to the load and to differ between clients, so that they do not all return at once. It also recommends that an agent keep no more than 10 outstanding requests per session, and no more than 10 outstanding requests that are not related to a session.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP control messages travel over TCP, so nothing is lost on the way and the connection can stay open for the whole session. If the other side is slow to answer, it says it is still working on it, and if it stays silent for 10 seconds the client gives up.

sections.title: The Methods
sections.content:
The method on a request says what to do to the resource named in the URI, and the method name is case sensitive. The RFC defines ten methods. OPTIONS asks what an agent supports and works in both directions. DESCRIBE fetches the description of a presentation or media object; the request and response pair forms the media initialization phase of RTSP. SETUP creates a session or changes the transport parameters of a stream that is already set up, and its response must carry the Accept-Ranges and Media-Properties headers, plus Media-Range for time-progressing media.

PLAY starts delivery. The server positions playback at the start of the requested Range, within the limits of the media and in accordance with the Seek-Style header, and always includes a Range header in its response with the actual start point. For RTP the RTP-Info header carries the synchronization data. A range outside the media gets 457 (Invalid Range). A PLAY that arrives while the session is already playing takes effect at once: a range with an explicit start replaces the current play, while a range with an implicit start such as npt=-25 only moves the end point. In an aggregated session, PLAY must use the aggregate control URI, otherwise the answer is 460 (Only Aggregate Operation Allowed).

PAUSE halts delivery immediately, and the response reports what remains of the range with a Range header. A later PLAY without a Range resumes from the pause point. When playback reaches the end of the media, the session stays in the Play state; only a PAUSE leaves it, because the state machine deliberately avoids automatic transitions.

Servers can send requests as well. PLAY_NOTIFY informs the client of an asynchronous event during play, with the reasons end-of-stream, media-properties-update and scale-change. REDIRECT tells a client to move to another server, with a required Terminate-Reason header and a Location header. A server with nowhere to redirect to uses TEARDOWN instead. GET_PARAMETER and SET_PARAMETER read and write parameters, and SET_PARAMETER is also the recommended keep-alive. An agent that does not support a method must return 501 (Not Implemented).

A client TEARDOWN on the aggregate control URI ends the session, and the response then carries no Session header. A TEARDOWN on one media URI inside an aggregated session is allowed only in the Ready state, and it removes just that stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request names one action and the stream it applies to. The client sets the session up, starts it, pauses it and takes it down. The server can also send requests, to announce that the media has ended or to send the client to a different server.

sections.title: The Session State Machine
sections.content:
Appendix B gives an informative state machine for each session, best read as the state of the server. There are three states. Init means no session exists, Ready means the session is ready to start playing, and Play means media is flowing from server to client. A correct SETUP moves Init to Ready, PLAY moves Ready to Play, and PAUSE moves Play back to Ready. A TEARDOWN of the whole presentation, a session timeout, or a REDIRECT without a time parameter returns the session to Init.

The state machine deliberately avoids automatic transitions. When all media has finished playing, the session still stays in the Play state until the client sends a PAUSE. In the Play state a SETUP for a new stream is refused with 455 (Method Not Valid in This State), and so is a TEARDOWN of a single media URI in an aggregated session. A SETUP for a stream that is already set up may change its transport parameters if the server supports that, and the response then carries a Range header and, for RTP, an RTP-Info header saying at what point the change takes effect.

The RFC states that where this appendix and the earlier sections disagree, the earlier sections win.
sections.plainLanguage: Each session sits in one of three states: no session, ready to play, or playing. Only a client request moves it between them, so a finished video does not change the state on its own.

sections.title: Media Delivery and Interleaved Binary Data
sections.content:
RTSP does not carry media in its basic form. The RFC specifies delivery with RTP over UDP, over TCP, or over the RTSP connection itself, and leaves room for other protocols to be added later. Appendix C defines the combinations of RTP profiles and lower-layer transports and how the Transport header describes them, including the use of RTCP for feedback and as a keep-alive. With RTP over UDP, one UDP flow carries RTP and a second carries RTCP, unless the two are multiplexed onto a single flow, which then carries both.

When a network blocks UDP, for example behind a network address translator, media can be interleaved with the RTSP messages on the same TCP connection. The RFC says this should generally be avoided unless necessary, because it complicates client and server operation and brings head-of-line blocking. Each block starts with an ASCII dollar sign (36), a one-octet channel identifier and a two-octet length, followed by exactly one upper-layer data unit such as one RTP packet. The channel numbers come from the interleaved parameter of the Transport header. When RTCP is used, it goes on the next channel up, and both channels carry traffic in both directions. Because the length is two octets, a block cannot exceed 65535 octets, which matches the maximum payload size of ordinary, non-jumbo IP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the video and the control messages travel separately. When the network blocks the video path, the video can be wrapped in small labelled blocks and sent along the control connection instead.

sections.title: Authentication, TLS and Threats
sections.content:
RTSP reuses the HTTP security framework. Servers should implement both Basic and Digest authentication, and clients must implement both. The RFC stresses that HTTP authentication alone does not provide full message security, so TLS should be used, and a message carrying Basic credentials must travel over a TLS connection with confidentiality protection enabled. Agents must implement RTSP over TLS, which is signalled by the rtsps scheme and its default port 322. If a client tries rtsp where the policy for the resource requires a secure channel, the server must answer with a 301 redirect to the correct rtsps URI.

Proxies are a special case, because a proxy acts as a man in the middle. The client can send an Accept-Credentials header to tell proxies how to treat the certificate of the next hop: Any, which accepts whatever is presented, Proxy, which is the default and lets the proxy apply its own policy, or User, where the proxy returns the certificate chain and the client decides. A proxy that cannot establish the next-hop TLS connection answers 472 (Failure to Establish Secure Connection).

The authentication mechanism covers client-to-server requests only. Server-to-client requests outside TLS are more exposed to message injection: REDIRECT to hijacking, TEARDOWN and PLAY_NOTIFY to denial of service.

The security considerations also cover session hijacking, which is reduced by large, random and non-sequential session identifiers, and resource exhaustion by servers that hold state. A remote denial-of-service attack is possible because a client can name another address as the media destination in a SETUP request. A server must therefore only allow client-specified destinations once it has ensured that the specified destination accepts receiving media. Media confidentiality and integrity are left to the media transport protocol, and the RFC points to Secure RTP (SRTP) for RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A password proves who the client is, and TLS protects the control messages so that nobody can read or change them. A server must check that a destination really accepts the media before it sends it there, because otherwise it could be used to flood somebody else's address.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MEDIA PROPERTIES THE SERVER REPORTS

items.title: Random access
items.text: Random-Access, Beginning-Only or No-Seeking, with the worst-case distance to a reachable point.

items.title: Retention
items.text: Unlimited, Time-Limited or Time-Duration, which decides how long the server keeps the media.

items.title: Content modification
items.text: Immutable, Dynamic or Time-Progressing, which says whether the content changes while the session runs.

items.title: Scales
items.text: The list of playback speeds that the content supports.

items.label: OPTIONS
items.desc: Asks what an agent supports. Works in both directions.

items.label: DESCRIBE
items.desc: Returns the presentation description of a resource.

items.label: SETUP
items.desc: Creates a session or changes the transport parameters of a stream.

items.label: PLAY
items.desc: Starts delivery, at the point named in the Range header.

items.label: PAUSE
items.desc: Halts delivery and keeps the pause point.

items.label: TEARDOWN
items.desc: Stops delivery and frees the resources of the session.

items.label: PLAY_NOTIFY
items.desc: Server-to-client notice of an event during play, such as the end of the media.

items.label: REDIRECT
items.desc: Server-to-client request to move the session to another server.

items.label: SET_PARAMETER
items.desc: Writes parameter values, and is the recommended keep-alive.
